newsitem.title: USA: Women say U.S. Army sex probe used coercion.
newsitem.headline: Women say U.S. Army sex probe used coercion.

text.p: Five female soldiers from the Army's Aberdeen Proving Ground said on Tuesday investigators had coerced them to make statements that they had been raped by higher-ranking soldiers.

"They tried to make me say 'rape' and I would not do it," Pvt. Kathryn Leming told a news conference at the home of a local representative of the National Association for the Advancement of Coloured People.

NAACP President Kweisi Mfume, also speaking at the news conference, called for an independent investigation of the issue of sexual harassment in the military, saying civil rights may have been violated in the probe.
"There are possible civil rights violations on behalf of the accusers and the accused that ought to be looked at," Mfume said. "We think that it (the investigation) borders on illegality."
Defence Department officials said they would look into the allegations but denied there was any racial harassment.

Seven instructors at the base have been charged with rape or other sexual misconduct in a scandal that erupted last year and prompted an Army-wide investigation into sexual harassment. Two of the seven took early discharge in lieu of court-martials, while the other five were awaiting trial.
Local NAACP officials have said the prevalence of blacks among the accused and white women among the accusers raises concerns of discrimination.

Pvt. Toni Moreland told the news conference she had falsely stated she had had consensual sex with an instructor because investigators told her he would escape punishment if she made the statement. She said she retracted the statement 10 days later after consultation with a chaplain.

Moreland faces a court-martial for making a false statement. Army officials said last week, when her retraction first became public, that the sergeant who was the object of the allegations had not been charged. The other women said they had resisted attempts to get them to denounce targets of the probe.
A spokesman for the Aberdeen base said he was not familiar with the individual allegations of coercion but the Army would have no interest in eliciting testimony that would not stand up.
"It's not to our benefit to have people making false statements," spokesman John Yaquiant said.

In Washington, the Defence Department said the allegations by the women would be investigated but denied that the harassment cases were racially motivated or that excessive pressure was brought on women by Army investigators.
